narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance was a significant concern.

Next, your family income bracket worked in your favor. Coming from a lower-middle income background actually pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, since most accepted students come from higher income brackets.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and pushed the outcome back toward failure. A score of 24 is well below the average of 37 among accepted students, which the model interpreted as a clear risk for not passing the bar.

Taken together, your low third-year ranking and modest LSAT score outweighed the modest positive effect of your family background, leading the model to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Strengthening these two areas will have the biggest impact on future applications.
